Females of the Japanese goatfish, Upeneus japonicus, produce pelagic eggs following a spawning event, and each newly fertilised ovum is a small, transparent sphere with a diameter of approximately one millimeter. The resulting wet weight of these yolk-laden eggs has been estimated at roughly 0.00062 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00062 grams], a value consistent with the buoyant, high-surface-area morphology typical of planktonic teleost embryos. Following a brief period of incubation, yolk-sac larvae emerge and undergo a rapid lecithotrophic phase during which the yolk reserves are progressively absorbed. The exotrophic transition, marked by the onset of first exogenous feeding, occurs when the mouth gapes opening allows the capture of small planktonic prey, such as copepod nauplii. A prolonged period of juvenile growth then ensues, during which the young-of-year gradually accumulate somatic tissue. The fork length at which these immature individuals attain reproductive maturity, or puberty, has been determined to be 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. This value was derived from gonadal inspection of preserved specimens, which indicated that the onset of gametogenesis and vitellogenesis consistently occurs once this length threshold is crossed.

The ultimate fork length, representing the maximum size reached by the oldest and largest adults in the population, has been recorded at 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is achieved only after several years of sustained growth and is seldom observed in field surveys, as most harvested individuals are taken at smaller sizes. Corresponding to this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight, or the largest adult body mass documented for this species, is approximately 324 grams [Wwi = approximately 324 grams]. This relationship between length and mass follows a power-law scaling typical of many mullid fishes, where the exponent exceeds three, indicating that larger individuals are slightly heavier per unit length than smaller conspecifics. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, which is the body mass associated with the 14-centimeter fork length, has been calculated to be roughly 37.5 grams [Wwp = roughly 37.5 grams]. This value highlights the substantial increase in somatic mass that must occur between the onset of reproductive capability and the attainment of the ultimate size, a pattern reflecting an extended period of post-maturational growth.

Under the ambient thermal conditions characteristic of its temperate habitat, maintained at a relatively stable 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], the reproductive physiology of Upeneus japonicus operates at a specific maximum rate. Gravid females, during the peak of the spawning season, are capable of releasing fertilised eggs at a remarkably high frequency. Based on field collections of actively spawning individuals and comparisons with the closely related congener Upeneus moluccensis, the maximum daily reproduction rate has been estimated at 473.5 eggs per day [Ri = 473.5 eggs per day]. This sustained output is achieved through multiple daily spawning events and relies on the continuous production and hydration of oocytes. The thermal dependence of this process is pronounced; at lower ambient temperatures, the rate of yolk deposition and egg maturation slows considerably, thereby capping daily fecundity at a fraction of the value observed at 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. This temperature effect underscores the role of environmental conditions in shaping the reproductive potential of this species.

The lifespan of the Japanese goatfish, based on extensive analysis of otolith growth increments and tag-recapture data collected from wild populations, has been determined to be 5 years [am = 5 years] under natural conditions at a stable temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. This maximum documented longevity indicates that the species follows a relatively fast life-history strategy for a teleost of its ultimate size, with a short generation time and a high turnover rate. Most individuals, however, experience natural mortality from predation or fishing pressure long before reaching this age, and the average lifespan in exploited populations is considerably shorter. The senescent phase, when it is observed in protected individuals, is characterized by a decline in gonad condition and a gradual loss of body condition, culminating in age-related death after the completion of the fifth year of life. The maximum recorded longevity of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days] provides a key parameter for demographic models used to assess the resilience of this species to fishing pressure at a temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C].

Beyond the static life-history parameters discussed above, the dynamic interplay between growth and reproduction in Upeneus japonicus reveals a pattern of indeterminate somatic expansion. Individuals that attain the fork length of 28 cm [Li = 28 cm] are exceptionally rare and represent the extreme upper tail of the size distribution, a testament to the slow growth rate characteristic of the post-maturational phase. Similarly, the maximum wet weight of 324 grams [Wwi = 324 grams] is a benchmark seldom reached, and most spawning adults encountered in trawl surveys weigh considerably less, typically falling within a range that brackets the 37.5 grams [Wwp = 37.5 grams] value. A comparative analysis with related species within the family Mullidae reveals that the daily reproductive output of approximately 473 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 473 eggs per day] is relatively high for a fish of this size, suggesting a specialized adaptation to maximize fecundity despite a moderate body size. Furthermore, the wet weight at birth, measured at 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams], is consistent with the minimal egg size strategy that allows the production of numerous offspring at each spawning event. The 5 year [am = 5 year] lifespan thus encapsulates a life cycle that prioritizes early maturity and high reproductive effort over extended individual survival, a common strategy among demersal fishes inhabiting productive continental shelf environments at a temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C].
